narrative:
The model put your estimated chance of leaving at 45%, and in this promotion process that was treated as a leave-risk prediction, so you were denied. This is a probability, not a certainty: it means the model saw a meaningful retention risk, not that your departure is guaranteed.

The strongest reason was your indication that you have other job opportunities. Only about one in four colleagues predicted to stay reported the same, so this was the main signal pushing the estimate toward leaving. The next most important factor was your six-to-ten years with this organization. That worked in your favor, pulling you toward staying, and it is a relatively common tenure among employees predicted to stay. The third key factor was your six-to-ten years of overall work experience. This pushed toward leaving, likely because mid-career experience can make outside moves easier, even though it is not unusual among stayers. Other concerns such as no annual bonus, low job support, no recognition, low job stability and psychological exhaustion add context, but they were not the top three drivers.

Before finalizing the decision, your manager should discuss your intent to stay, clarify promotion criteria and career path, and address practical retention levers such as recognition, support, stability and bonus. You should also state what would make you stay; the organization should revisit the denial if that risk can be credibly reduced.
